## Where This Fits
This week replaces the mechanism behind two ledger entries nobody has touched yet. The first is the **$2N$ on the weight side**: W7 will show loss falling with $N$, but a dense model pays two FLOPs per token for every parameter it adds — MoE splits $N$ into $N_{\text{total}}$ (memory and knowledge capacity) and $N_{\text{active}}$ (FLOPs per token); that row has been on the ledger since W1, and this week it gets numbers. The second is the **KV on the attention side**: W5's "long context" row says $M_{\text{KV}} \propto L$ and decode's attention side $\propto L$; W3's GQA/MLA shrank the constant and W5's sparse attention changed which keys are read, and this week replaces what produces the KV at all — linear attention and state-space models keep a **fixed-size state** instead of a cache that grows with every token (W2's retina metaphor: "the memory behind the eye has a resolution too"; W1's closing: a fixed-size state is an asset at inference, paid for in copying and recall). The week's one mathematical thread is **associativity**: once softmax is gone, $(\phi(\mathbf{Q})\phi(\mathbf{K})^\top)\mathbf{V}$ can be computed as $\phi(\mathbf{Q})(\phi(\mathbf{K})^\top\mathbf{V})$, which gives the recurrence, the fixed state, and Mamba-2's "one operation, two algorithms" (a recurrence or a matrix product); RetNet, GLA, Mamba-2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet and KDA from 2023–2025 are one recurrence $\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{G}_t\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{k}_t\mathbf{v}_t^\top$ with different choices of $\mathbf{G}_t$. The third part is the state of play in 2026, and it has **not converged**: hybrid-linear (Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear, Nemotron-H, Falcon-H1, and KDA inside Kimi K3), sparse (DeepSeek-V3.2/V4, W5's budget view) and a return to full attention (the MiniMax-M2 team's post) are all shipping at once — which makes this the week with the densest training in reading evidence: the comparison conditions of an architecture paper (iso-FLOPs? iso-parameters? iso-latency?) almost decide its conclusion. If the course is behind, this week can be compressed, but **the activation-ratio trend of MoE and the associativity of linear attention cannot be cut**: the first is the ticket to reading a 2026 open-weight `config.json`, the second is the mathematical root of W11's inference efficiency and of every "fixed state" argument before W14. **The two algorithms of linear attention are written live by the instructor** (demo 3); the MoE collapse and the hybrid-versus-full comparison are rehearsed in advance and replayed in class. You do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. From an MoE `config.json` (`num_experts`, `num_experts_per_tok`, `moe_intermediate_size`, shared experts), compute $N_{\text{total}}$ and $N_{\text{active}}$ with W4's parameter accounting, define the activation ratio $\rho = N_{\text{active}}/N_{\text{total}}$, and use "total parameters set memory, active parameters set FLOPs" to say where MoE moves the cost (→ memory capacity, all-to-all communication between experts, router quality); for the 2024–2026 flagships, state the trend of $\rho$ falling from about 5.5% towards 3% and the design direction behind it (more, smaller experts).
2. Write the forward pass of top-$k$ routing and the Switch-style load-balancing loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha\, n_E \sum_i f_i P_i$; explain why it conflicts with the main loss (it pushes the router towards uniformity regardless of content), why experts collapse without any balancing term (the chosen expert trains better and gets chosen more), and what the auxiliary-loss-free per-expert bias (it changes the selection only, not the gate value, and never enters the loss) is solving.
3. Derive the associativity of linear attention on the board: $(\phi(\mathbf{Q})\phi(\mathbf{K})^\top)\mathbf{V}$ and $\phi(\mathbf{Q})(\phi(\mathbf{K})^\top\mathbf{V})$ are equal in mathematics and differ in computation, $O(L^2 d_{\text{head}})$ against $O(L\,d_{\text{head}}^2)$; from the causal version derive the recurrence $\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \phi(\mathbf{k}_t)\mathbf{v}_t^\top$, $\mathbf{o}_t = \mathbf{S}_t^\top\phi(\mathbf{q}_t)$, state that $\mathbf{S}_t$ is a $d_{\text{head}} \times d_{\text{head}}$ state independent of $L$; and **compute its capacity** — at most $d_{\text{head}}$ key–value pairs stored orthogonally, with interference beyond that — the mathematical reason precise recall weakens.
4. Write the 2023–2025 recurrence family as one equation $\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{G}_t\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{k}_t\mathbf{v}_t^\top$ and fill the table: RetNet (a fixed scalar decay), Mamba-2/SSD (an input-dependent scalar $\gamma_t$), GLA (a per-dimension vector gate), DeltaNet ($\mathbf{G}_t = \mathbf{I} - \beta_t\mathbf{k}_t\mathbf{k}_t^\top$, one step of online gradient descent: erase the old value before writing), Gated DeltaNet and KDA (both combined); say what Mamba's selective mechanism ($\mathbf{B}_t, \mathbf{C}_t, \Delta_t$ as functions of the input) changes relative to S4; and give the skeleton of state-space duality: unroll the recurrence into a matrix product with a decay mask, the mask is semiseparable, so within a chunk use the matrix product and across chunks the recurrence — **matmul for training, recurrence for inference**, which is exactly what mlx-lm's `ssm.py` does.
5. Explain what each of the three 2026 routes attacks and what it pays: hybrid-linear (most layers a fixed state, a few layers full attention for precise recall; Qwen3-Next's 3:1 comes from the model card and `config.json`, Kimi Linear's from the body (§4, §5.2) and `config.json` — neither from an abstract — and the 7% attention of Waleffe et al. from the abstract), sparse (DeepSeek-V3.2/V4: change which keys are read, the KV stays, W5), and a return to full attention (the MiniMax-M2 team's reasons: evaluation cannot see the gap, linear attention is more sensitive to numerical precision, the infrastructure is immature) — and say that these three routes **have not converged**, and that the layer ratio is still a hyperparameter without a principle.
6. Diagnose the comparison conditions of an architecture paper: first ask what each row of the table holds fixed (iso-FLOPs, iso-parameters, iso-latency, iso-tokens, the same tokenizer), say how the conclusion flips with the condition (MoE beats dense at iso-FLOPs and loses at iso-parameters; linear beats full on throughput and depends on the hybrid ratio on recall tasks), and for Kimi Linear's "beats full attention under a fair comparison" say what it held fixed and what it did not.

## Demos
The programs for this week's demos, published as they are built. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|----------------------|-------|----------------------------------------------|---------------|----------|
| [**Demo 1**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w06_d1_activation_ratio)<br>[The activation ratio, from `config.json`]{.demo-sub} | p10–p11 | **Why:** the one number that says what a mixture of experts buys and what it costs — $N_{\text{total}}$ sets memory, $N_{\text{active}}$ sets FLOPs — computed from the config files of four real models, with the safetensors headers as the check.<br>**What you see:** two columns per model, the formula from `config.json` against the tensor shapes read from each shard's header (no weights are downloaded); the keys that name the experts differ from one family to the next, and the file settles what the config does not say.<br>**Result:** Gemma 4 26B-A4B 25.23 B / 3.82 B / 15.2 % (every layer runs a dense FFN *and* 128 experts); Qwen3-30B-A3B 30.53 B / 3.35 B / 11.0 % (the two columns agree to the parameter); Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B 79.67 B / 3.87 B / 4.9 % (a 1.65 B MTP module in the checkpoint, excluded); Kimi Linear 48B-A3B 49.12 B / 3.48 B / 7.1 %. In every case the attention and embedding floor is about half of $N_{\text{active}}$ | standard library only; `fetch` needs the network once (headers, a few MB) | any laptop  |
| [**Demo 2**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w06_d2_moe_balance)<br>[Three ways to balance a mixture of experts]{.demo-sub} | p16–p17 | **Why:** watch expert collapse happen, and what two fixes do about it, on a model small enough to train three times.<br>**What you see:** W4's character-level tiny GPT with every feed-forward block replaced by an MoE layer ($n_E = 8$, $k = 2$, the same expert parameters per token as the dense block), trained three times from the same initialisation — no balancing term; Switch's auxiliary loss with $\alpha = 10^{-2}$; the auxiliary-loss-free bias — with the per-expert load and the held-out loss recorded every 25 steps and replayed.<br>**Result:** without a balancing term every layer collapses onto two experts within 25 steps — inside the warmup — and after 3000 steps two layers are still there (largest share 0.5, six of eight experts starved; 0.397 averaged over layers). Switch's loss balances within 100 steps (0.151 against the ideal 0.125, nobody starved) and pays 0.055 nats/char of held-out loss for it. The bias collapses exactly like the first run, then pulls back at 0.001 per step — level by 1500 steps, 0.147 at the end — at a cost of 0.029 nats. One seed; the shape of a mechanism, not a threshold | `torch` only; training on `mps` (60 / 36 / 43 min for the three runs), `replay` needs nothing | Apple silicon as tested; any machine with `torch` for `replay`  |
| [**Demo 3**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w06_d3_linear_scratch)<br>[Linear attention from scratch: two algorithms, a recurrence, a notebook]{.demo-sub} | p23–p24 | **Why:** the two claims of the blackboard derivation — the two bracketings are equal in mathematics and different in computation, and a fixed-size state can hold at most $d_{\text{head}}$ pairs cleanly — each turned into a number by a few lines of code.<br>**What you see:** seven functions written live in plain `torch` (CPU, float64), a test after each: the two orderings on random inputs; their running times at $d_{\text{head}} = 128$ for $L$ from 32 to 8192; the causal recurrence against a one-shot `cumsum`; and a $128 \times 128$ notebook filled with $m$ key–value pairs and read back — with orthogonal keys, with random keys, and with random keys written by the delta rule.<br>**Result:** the two orderings agree to $1.6 \times 10^{-15}$ relative; the recurrence matches the closed form to $1.2 \times 10^{-15}$; on the CPU the two timing lines cross between $L = 32$ and $L = 128$ — level at $L = 128$, the theoretical point — and linear is $28\times$ faster at $L = 8192$ (86 ms against 3.0 ms; the ratio moves with the machine, the crossover region did not between two machines). Orthogonal keys read back exactly up to $m = 128$ and fail from the 129th pair (0.62 at $m = 160$); random keys are off by 0.50 already at $m = 32$ and 1.00 at $m = 128$ — the same as $\sqrt{(m-1)/128}$ to two decimals, no knee; the delta rule lowers every point (0.74 at $m = 128$) but keeps the bound. Writing the same key twice: additive recall is $\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2$, delta recall is $\mathbf{v}_2$ | `torch` only; about a second; no model, no network | any laptop  |
| [**Demo 4**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w06_d4_hybrid_vs_full)<br>[A parallel hybrid against full attention: cache against $L$, and recall]{.demo-sub} | p36–p37 | **Why:** the cost accounting of p34–p35 on two real models of comparable size — Falcon-H1-7B-Instruct, a parallel hybrid with a Mamba-2 block and an attention block in every layer, against Qwen3-8B with full attention — and the one question the accounting cannot answer: what the hybrid's smaller attention costs it in retrieval.<br>**What you see:** (a) W3 demo 2's measurement, prompts of 1k to 32k tokens, with the cache of each hybrid layer split into the keys and values that grow with $L$ and the SSM and convolution states that do not, against the formula lines; (b) W5 demo 3's key–value retrieval with the same $K$ and the same questions, ten cells per model, two or three questions put to both models live.<br>**Result:** (a) both lines sit on their formulas to the byte: Qwen3-8B 144 KiB per token (4.50 GiB at 32k), Falcon-H1 44 KiB per token plus a fixed 132.9 MiB (the fp32 SSM state of 44 layers, the same at every length; 1.51 GiB at 32k) — a slope ratio of 3.27 and a line that starts *above* Qwen3's and crosses it near 1.3k tokens. Prefill time did not follow the cache: 19.1 s against 18.5 s at 32k. (b) Under these two tokenizers the same JSON is 5.6k and 22k tokens, not 4k and 16k. Qwen3-8B: 15 · 16 · 17 · 17 · 20 of 20 at 5.6k and 16 · 5 · 3 · 3 · 19 at 22k — the U-shape of Liu et al., deep in the middle, on the very questions that Llama 3.1 8B answered 200 of 200 in W5. Falcon-H1-7B: 0 of 200, and not one reply was a UUID — fragments of hex and filler prose — so the hybrid's retrieval was not measured, only its failure to generate; a short probe showed it answers plain English but cannot copy even a single UUID verbatim, so the failure is in reproducing hex strings, independent of context length; whether the 4-bit MLX port or the model is the cause is open | `mlx`, `mlx-lm`; two 4-bit models (≈ 9 GB); `fetch` once for Falcon-H1; (b) about 35–40 min per model | Apple silicon only  |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.0, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese.

## References
- **Textbooks**: no textbook chapter covers this week (JM3's ch 7, 2026-08-19 release, treats the dense Transformer only — table of contents checked 2026-10-18: no section on MoE, SSMs or linear attention; MoE is mentioned once, in passing, in §7.8); Sun et al.'s survey stands in as the reading
- **Mixture of Experts**
- Shazeer et al., **Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer**, arXiv:1701.06538 (2017) — where the sparsely-gated MoE layer and its trainable gating begin; the abstract: thousands of feed-forward sub-networks, capacity up by more than 1000×
- Lepikhin et al., **GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding**, arXiv:2006.16668 (2020) — a 600B-parameter MoE translation model; the family of load-balancing losses starts here
- Fedus, Zoph & Shazeer, **Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity**, JMLR 23(120), 2022 (arXiv:2101.03961) — top-1 routing; the source of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha\,n_E\sum_i f_i P_i$
- Zoph et al., **ST-MoE: Designing Stable and Transferable Sparse Expert Models**, arXiv:2202.08906 (2022) — the router z-loss (body); the abstract: a 269B sparse model trained at the compute of a 32B dense one
- Jiang et al., **Mixtral of Experts**, arXiv:2401.04088 (2024) — eight experts, two chosen per token; 47B total / 13B active (abstract); the routing analysis in §5 is the source of "experts are not domain experts"
- Dai et al., **DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models**, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2401.06066; Anthology 2024.acl-long.70) — the source of fine-grained and shared experts; the design root of the falling activation ratio
- Wang et al., **Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing Strategy for Mixture-of-Experts**, arXiv:2408.15664 (2024) — a per-expert bias that changes the selection only and never enters the loss (abstract); adopted by DeepSeek-V3
- DeepSeek-AI, **DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report**, arXiv:2412.19437 (2024; v2 February 2025) — 671B/37B, auxiliary-loss-free balancing and MTP are all in the abstract; **the MoE section (§2) is taken apart in class this week**
- Clark et al., **Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models**, ICML 2022 (PMLR 162; arXiv:2202.01169) — two-axis scaling laws for MoE and the effective parameter count
- Ludziejewski et al., **Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2402.07871, where Krajewski is listed first) — granularity enters the scaling law; "expert width = FFN width" is not optimal at almost any budget (abstract)
- Abnar et al., **Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models**, ICML 2025 (PMLR 267; arXiv:2501.12370) — at fixed compute there is an optimal sparsity (abstract); that it rises with the budget is in the body
- **Linear attention and the recurrence family**
- Katharopoulos et al., **Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention**, ICML 2020 (PMLR 119; arXiv:2006.16236) — the original source of the associativity argument; the one on the board this week
- Sun et al., **Retentive Network: A Successor to Transformer for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2307.08621 (2023) — a recurrence with a fixed decay; **an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed**
- Yang et al., **Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2312.06635) — per-dimension gates and the chunked algorithm (FlashLinearAttention)
- Yang et al., **Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2406.06484) — chunk-parallel training with the delta rule; at 1.3B it beats Mamba and GLA (abstract)
- Yang, Kautz & Hatamizadeh, **Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2412.06464) — gating and the delta rule are complementary (abstract); the linear layer Qwen3-Next ships
- Sun et al., **Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States**, ICML 2025 (PMLR 267; arXiv:2407.04620) — the state is a small model and the update is one self-supervised learning step (abstract); the delta rule generalised
- Arora et al., **Simple linear attention language models balance the recall-throughput tradeoff**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2402.18668) — the trade-off between recall and state size; BASED
- Arora et al., **Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2312.04927) and Jelassi et al., **Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2402.01032) — cited in W1: what a fixed state costs in associative recall and copying; this week's capacity argument leads back to both
- **State-space models**
- Gu, Goel & Ré, **Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces**, ICLR 2022, Outstanding Paper Honorable Mention (arXiv:2111.00396) — S4
- Gu & Dao, **Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces**, COLM 2024 (arXiv:2312.00752) — the selective mechanism; the abstract: letting the SSM parameters depend on the input removes the weakness on discrete modalities
- Dao & Gu, **Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2405.21060) — Mamba-2 and SSD; **assigned reading this week: §6, the SSD algorithm**
- Feng et al., **Were RNNs All We Needed?**, arXiv:2410.01201 (2024) — minLSTM and minGRU train in parallel; cited in W1; **an arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed**
- **Hybrids and the three routes of 2025–2026**
- Lieber et al., **Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model**, arXiv:2403.19887 (2024) — the first shipped interleaved hybrid with MoE; the layer ratio is in the body
- Waleffe et al., **An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models**, arXiv:2406.07887 (2024) — a controlled comparison at 8B and 3.5T tokens: a hybrid of 43% Mamba-2, 7% attention and 50% MLP layers exceeds the 8B Transformer on all 12 standard tasks (abstract)
- NVIDIA, **Nemotron-H: A Family of Accurate and Efficient Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models**, arXiv:2504.03624 (2025; v4 September 2025) — replaces the majority of self-attention layers with Mamba (abstract)
- Zuo et al., **Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance**, arXiv:2507.22448 (2025) — a **parallel** hybrid (abstract: a parallel hybrid of attention and SSMs); 0.5B to 34B; the model of demo 4; native in mlx-lm
- Du et al., **Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture**, arXiv:2510.26692 (2025) — **assigned reading this week**: KDA (delta rule plus per-dimension gating, a DPLR chunked algorithm) in a layerwise hybrid with MLA, 48B/3B; claims to beat full MLA under a fair comparison and to cut the KV cache by 75% (abstract); what the fair comparison holds fixed is in §5.4: the KDA hybrid, the all-MLA model and the GDN hybrid share the same architecture, parameter count (48B/3B) and training setup, 1.4T tokens, a 4,096-token pre-training window; the §5.2 ablation (same FLOPs budget and hyperparameters) selects 3:1 among 0:1, 1:1, 3:1, 7:1 and 15:1 by perplexity, where pure full attention (0:1) performs worst; the 3:1 layer ratio is not in the abstract but in the body (§4 and the §5.2 ablation) and in `config.json` (20 KDA layers to 7 MLA)
- Kimi Team, **Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence**, arXiv:2607.24653 (2026) — 2.8T/104B, KDA and Attention Residuals, 16 of 896 routed experts active (abstract); the shipping record of KDA in a flagship; **licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, mind this for classroom use**
- Qwen Team, **Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B** model card and the blog post "Qwen3-Next: Towards Ultimate Training & Inference Efficiency" (September 2025) — **a model card and a blog post, not a paper; Qwen3-Next has no technical report**: Gated DeltaNet and gated attention interleaved 3:1, 512 experts with 10 active plus one shared, MTP
- Wu et al., **MiniMax-01: Scaling Foundation Models with Lightning Attention**, arXiv:2501.08313 (2025) — 456B/45.9B, lightning attention with MoE (abstract); the ratio of linear to softmax layers is in the body
- Chen et al., **The MiniMax-M2 Series: Mini Activations Unleashing Max Real-World Intelligence**, arXiv:2605.26494 (2026) — 229.9B/9.8B (abstract); the abstract **says nothing about the form of attention**
- MiniMax, **Why Did M2 End Up as a Full Attention Model?**, team post of 2025-10-29 (on behalf of pre-training lead Haohai Sun) — **a company post, not a paper**; three reasons for returning to full attention: evaluation cannot see the gap, linear attention is more sensitive to numerical precision, the infrastructure is immature
- **The DeepSeek line (the MoE section of V3 is taken apart in class; the rest is self-study; the sparse branch is W5's budget view)**
- **DeepSeek-V2**, arXiv:2405.04434 (MLA first appears; 236B/21B; cited in W3) → **DeepSeek-V3**, arXiv:2412.19437 → **DeepSeek-V3.2**, arXiv:2512.02556 (DSA; cited in W5) → **DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence**, arXiv:2606.19348 (a hybrid attention of CSA and HCA, mHC, Muon; Pro 1.6T/49B, Flash 284B/13B — all in the abstract)
- **Other open-weight lines (landscape, not to be read paper by paper)**: Yang et al., **Qwen3 Technical Report**, arXiv:2505.09388 (0.6B–235B, Apache 2.0 stated in the abstract; the default model family of this course's labs); Bai et al., **Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence**, arXiv:2507.20534 (1T/32B, MuonClip); GLM-4.5 Team, **GLM-4.5: Agentic, Reasoning, and Coding (ARC) Foundation Models**, arXiv:2508.06471 (355B/32B)
- **Survey**: Sun et al., **Speed Always Wins: A Survey on Efficient Architectures for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2508.09834 (2025; still v1 as of October 2026) — covers linear and sparse sequence modelling, efficient attention, sparse MoE and hybrids; **still the only architecture survey with enough coverage**
- He et al., **Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference**, Thinking Machines Lab blog, September 2025 — **a company blog post, not a paper**; the main reason temperature = 0 is still not deterministic is that kernels lack batch invariance; developed in W11
- Meta AI, **The Llama 4 herd**, April 2025 blog post — cited in W5; Llama 4 has no technical report, so its MoE design can only be cited from the blog

> **Two absences to make explicit in class**: **Qwen3-Next has no technical report** (only a blog post and a model card), yet it is widely used as a baseline in 2026 papers; **neither does Llama 4**. Their designs can only be cited from model cards, and the slides say so. **Open weights are not open methods.**
